cse-2021-1-cs-13.approach: Without checkpoints, the log is the only record of what to undo/redo, and log-based undo/redo operations are idempotent; so a second recovery simply rebuilds its lists from the same log and runs again.

steps.title: Where the lists come from
steps.body: After a crash the recovery manager scans the log: transactions with `<T start>` and `<T commit>` go to the **redo list**, those with `<T start>` but no commit go to the **undo list**. With no checkpoint written (neither during normal work nor during recovery), the second recovery scans the same log from the beginning and builds the **same undo and redo lists** — (A).

steps.title: Why recovery still succeeds
steps.body: Redo writes the new value and undo writes the old value logged for each update. Doing this twice gives the same result as doing it once (idempotent), so a crash in the middle of recovery is harmless: the system just recovers again. So (B) and (D) are false.

steps.title: Statement C
steps.body: The stored key also includes (C), read as: work that the interrupted recovery has already completed does not need to be recovered as a separate, extra step — the restarted recovery just reapplies the same lists, which leaves those items unchanged. (Read literally, the restarted recovery does re-run idempotent operations over them, which is why this statement is debated.)

optionAnalysis.reason: No checkpoint means the same log scan produces the same undo and redo lists.
Undo/redo are idempotent, so recovery can simply be restarted.
Included in the stored key: already undone/redone work needs no separate recovery; reapplying idempotent operations changes nothing.
Once recovery completes the database is consistent; a repeated crash does not corrupt it.

pitfalls: Thinking a crash during recovery is unrecoverable — idempotent redo/undo make restarting safe.
cse-2021-1-cs-13.verification: The log is unchanged except for appended records, and with no checkpoint the restart scans it from the start, giving identical lists; idempotence makes repeated application safe.

cse-2021-1-cs-14.approach: A library call always enters the kernel only if its job inherently needs a kernel service every time; check each function for a path that stays in user space.

steps.title: Always kernel
steps.body: `exit` must terminate the process, which only the kernel can do (it ends in the `_exit`/`exit_group` system call). `sleep` must block the process for a time, which needs the scheduler (`nanosleep` system call). Both always trap into the kernel.

steps.title: Not always
steps.body: `malloc` serves most requests from the heap already obtained by the process and calls `brk`/`mmap` only when the free pool is exhausted. `strlen` just walks bytes in user memory and never needs the kernel.

optionAnalysis.reason: Process termination is a kernel operation (`_exit`).
Small allocations come from the existing heap; `brk`/`mmap` only sometimes.
Suspending the process needs the kernel scheduler (`nanosleep`).
Pure user-space computation over a string.

pitfalls: Marking `malloc` as always making a system call — it is buffered by the allocator.
cse-2021-1-cs-14.verification: Tracing a loop of small `malloc` calls with strace shows only occasional `brk`/`mmap`, while every `sleep` shows `nanosleep` and `exit` shows `exit_group`.

cse-2021-1-cs-15.approach: In an unsorted linear list a scan can stop early when it finds the target, but proving a name is absent needs the whole list. So an operation needs a full scan exactly when it must check that some name does not already exist.

steps.title: Operations that must prove absence
steps.body: **Create**: the new name must not already be in `foo`, so every entry must be examined before appending. **Rename**: the new name must not clash with any existing file, so again every entry must be checked. Both need a full scan.

steps.title: Operations that look up one existing name
steps.body: **Delete** and **open** only need to locate the given file; the scan stops as soon as the name is found, which can be the first node. So a full scan is not necessary.

optionAnalysis.reason: Must confirm the name is not already present: whole list.
Stops once the file is found; may be the first node.
The new name must be checked against every entry for duplicates.
Search stops at the matching entry.

pitfalls: Forgetting that rename also has to enforce unique names in the directory.
cse-2021-1-cs-15.verification: Worst case vs necessary case: delete/open can succeed after one comparison; create/rename cannot succeed without comparing against all n entries.

cse-2021-1-cs-17.approach: Kruskal's view: take every 0.1 edge (they form no cycle), see how many components remain, and count the ways to join them with the cheapest available 0.9 edges.

steps.title: Take all 0.1 edges
steps.body: Name the grid rows a b c / d e f / g h i. The seven 0.1 edges are a–b, b–c, d–e, h–i, d–g, e–h, f–i. They form no cycle, so every MST contains all of them.

steps.title: Components left
steps.body: Two components remain: $\{a,b,c\}$ (top row) and $\{d,e,f,g,h,i\}$ (5 edges on 6 vertices, already a tree). We need $8 - 7 = 1$ more edge, of weight 0.9, joining them.

steps.title: Count the choices
steps.body: The 0.9 edges e–f and g–h lie inside the bottom component (they would make a cycle). The only crossing edges are the three verticals a–d, b–e, c–f, each of weight 0.9. Any one of them completes an MST, giving **3** minimum spanning trees of weight $7(0.1) + 0.9 = 1.6$.

pitfalls: Counting all 0.9 edges as candidates — e–f and g–h close cycles in the lower component.

cse-2021-1-cs-18.approach: For an exponential variable the tail is $P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$ and the mean is $1/\lambda$, so $P(X > E[X]) = e^{-1}$ whatever the parameter.

steps.title: Mean
steps.body: With rate $\lambda = 2$: $f(x) = 2e^{-2x}$ for $x \ge 0$ and $E[X] = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{2}$.

steps.title: Tail probability
steps.body: $P(X > \tfrac12) = \int_{1/2}^{\infty} 2e^{-2x}\,dx = e^{-2 \cdot \frac12} = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679 \approx 0.37$.

cse-2021-1-cs-18.shortcut: $P(X > E[X]) = e^{-\lambda \cdot (1/\lambda)} = e^{-1}$ — no need to know $\lambda$.
pitfalls: Reading "parameter 2" as the mean changes $E[X]$ but not the answer — it is still $e^{-1}$.

cse-2021-1-cs-19.approach: The two fixed jobs already give the fastest and slowest computers a job; only the middle computer can end up empty, so count assignments of the other 4 jobs and subtract those that skip it.

steps.title: Fix the forced jobs
steps.body: Toughest job → fastest computer, easiest job → slowest computer. These two computers are now non-empty. The remaining 4 jobs can go to any of the 3 computers: $3^4 = 81$ ways.

steps.title: Remove bad cases
steps.body: The only way to violate "every computer gets a job" is for the middle computer to get none, i.e. all 4 jobs go to the fastest or slowest: $2^4 = 16$ ways.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Valid assignments = all assignments of the 4 free jobs − those leaving the middle computer empty: $81 - 16 = 65$.

pitfalls: Treating jobs as identical or counting only how many jobs each computer gets (that gives a small number like 10).
cse-2021-1-cs-19.verification: Direct count by how many of the 4 free jobs the middle computer gets: $\binom41 2^3 + \binom42 2^2 + \binom43 2 + \binom44 = 32 + 24 + 8 + 1 = 65$ ✓.

cse-2021-1-cs-20.approach: The limit is $0/0$ and equals the derivative of $\sqrt{2x+22}$ at $x=-3$ (since $\sqrt{16}=4$); rationalising gives the same.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body: At $x=-3$: $\sqrt{-6+22} = \sqrt{16} = 4$, so the limit is $\dfrac{2}{4+4} = \dfrac14 = 0.25$.

cse-2021-1-cs-26.approach: Check what type each production assigns: the rule E → ID always sets int, ignoring the declared type, so only programs that use int variables are type-checked correctly.

steps.title: Spot the flaw
steps.body: `E → ID {set E.type := int}` never looks up the type recorded by the declaration. A variable declared `bool` is still treated as `int` in expressions.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body: For a bool variable `b`, `!b` would be rejected (E1.type is int, not bool), and `b + 1` would be wrongly accepted. So boolean declarations/expressions are mishandled and (A), (C) fail. If every variable is int, every type it assigns is right and `+` is checked correctly — (B).

steps.title: No infinite loop
steps.body: Actions are executed once per production during parsing/traversal; left recursion in E matters only for a top-down parser, not for the SDT actions themselves. (D) is false.

For int declarations and int expressions every assigned type is correct.

The actions are simple assignments/checks executed once per node.

cse-2021-1-cs-26.verification: Try `bool b; !b`: E → ID sets int, then `!` requires bool → spurious error, confirming bool checking is broken while int-only programs pass.

cse-2021-1-cs-30.approach: For $T(n) = T(an) + T(bn) + cn$ with $a + b < 1$, the work per level shrinks geometrically, so the root's $\Theta(n)$ dominates.

steps.title: Work per level
steps.body: Level 0 does $7n$. Level 1 does $7(\frac n2 + \frac{2n}{5}) = 7n \cdot \frac{9}{10}$. Level $k$ does at most $7n(\frac{9}{10})^k$.

steps.title: Sum
steps.body: $T(n) \le 7n \sum_{k \ge 0} (0.9)^k = 7n \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 0.9} = 70n$ (plus $O(n)$ leaves). Also $T(n) \ge 7n$. Hence $T(n) = \Theta(n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Far too large: total work is at most 70n.
n log n arises only when the fractions sum to exactly 1 (e.g. n/2 + n/2).
Geometric decrease by 9/10 per level gives Θ(n).
Sub-linear is impossible: the root alone costs 7n.

cse-2021-1-cs-33.approach: Join the fragments step by step; each join is lossless when the common attributes are a key (via the FDs) of one side. A fragment sharing no attributes with the rest makes the decomposition lossy.

steps.body: $(T,X)$ shares only $T$ or $X$ with nothing: the other fragments $PQS, QY, YZW$ contain neither $T$ nor $X$. Joining with no common attribute is a Cartesian product, so spurious tuples appear — $D_2$ is lossy.
